$$ \sigma\{\widetilde{V}_{1},\widetilde{V}_{2},\ldots,\widetilde{V}_{u-1},\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994ptH_{j,0},H_{j,1},\ldots,H_{j,u-1},\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994ptV^{(0)}_{j}\}. $$

However, $\widetilde{V}_{1},\widetilde{V}_{2},\ldots,\widetilde{V}_{u-1},\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(0)}_{j}$ are independent by Lemma 3.1. And also $H_{j,0},\ldots,H_{j,u}$ are independent from $\widetilde{V}_{i},\widetilde{V}_{i+1},\ldots,\widetilde{V}_{u-1},\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(0)}_{j}.$ Hence, the collection

$$ \{\widetilde{V}_{1},\widetilde{V}_{2},\ldots,\widetilde{V}_{u-1},\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(0)}_{j},H_{j,0},H_{j,1},\ldots,H_{j,u-1},H_{j,u}\} $$

is jointly independent and so $H_{ju},\widetilde{V}_{u}$ are independent of the sigma algebra generated by $\{\widetilde{V}_{i},\widetilde{V}_{i+1},\ldots,\widetilde{V}_{u-1},H_{j,0},H_{j,1},\ldots,H_{j,u-1},V^{(0)}_{j}\},$ which makes $V^{(i-1)}_{j}$ measurable.

Going back to the problem, we have the martingale difference sum

$$ Q=\sum_{u=i+1}^{j-1}s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)-p. $$

Each term is bounded by 1 and has conditional variance $p-p^{2}\leq p.$ By Theorem 2.2 for $L=np$ and $a=1,$ the inequality $\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$[$}}}|Q|\geq z\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$]$}}}\leq 2\exp(-\frac{z^{2}/2}{np+z/3})$ holds. Take $z=100\max(\sqrt{np\log n},\log n).$ The number of non-zero terms is $Q+np\leq np+100C_{A}\max(\sqrt{np\log n},\log n)\leq 200C_{A}\max(np,\log n).$ ∎

#### Step 3: Martingale violations (V1).

We now deal with the term (Violations 1). Recall from (V1) that this term appears due to the rescaling in the direction orthogonal to $\widetilde{V}_{u}$ when flipping $V^{(u-1)}_{j}$ with respect to $\widetilde{V}_{u}.$ For each $u,$ by Propositions 4.1 and 4.3, with high probability $1-1/n^{100}$

$$ \vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\psi(\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\langle\widetilde{V}_{i},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\leq C^{\prime}\frac{\log^{3/2}n}{d^{3/2}} $$

for some absolute constant $C^{\prime}.$ Combining with Lemma 4.4, with probability $1-O(1/n^{100}),$

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\sum_{u=i+1}^{j-1}s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\psi(\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\langle\widetilde{V}_{i},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\Big| \displaystyle\leq\sum_{u=i+1}^{j-1}s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\Big|\psi(\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\langle\widetilde{V}_{i},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\Big|\leq C^{\prime}\max(np,\log n)\frac{\log^{3/2}n}{d^{3/2}} $$

When $d=\Omega(\max(np,\log n)),$ we have ${d^{-3/2}}{\max(np,\log n)\log^{3/2}n}={O({d^{-1}}\max(\sqrt{np},\sqrt{\log n})(\log n)^{3/2}}).$

#### Step 4: Martingale violations (V2).

Next, we consider the term in (Violations 2). As in (V2), it appears due to fact that $V^{(u-1)}_{j}$ and $\widetilde{V}_{i}$ are not independent. By Propositions 4.1 and 4.3, with high probability $1-1/n^{100}$ ,

$$ \Big|\kappa(\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\langle V^{(u-1)}_{j},\widetilde{V}_{i}\rangle\Big|\leq C^{\prime}\frac{\log^{3/2}n}{d^{3/2}}. $$

Using Lemma 4.4 we conclude that with probability $1-O(1/n^{100})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\sum_{u=i+1}^{j-1}s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\kappa\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$($}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$)$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\langle V^{(u-1)}_{j},\widetilde{V}_{i}\rangle\Big|\leq\frac{C^{\prime}\max(np,\log n)\log^{3/2}n}{d^{3/2}}. $$

Again, when $d=\Omega(\max(np,\log n)),$ this expression is of order $O(\max(\sqrt{np},\sqrt{\log n})\frac{(\log n)^{3/2}}{d}).$

#### Step 5: Truncating the martingale differences.

The remaining sum

$$ \sum_{u=i+1}^{j-1}s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\kappa(\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle $$

is a sum of martingale differences. However, we need to truncate it so that we have a small uniform bound to apply Freedman’s inequality Theorem 2.2. To this end, we write

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{u=i+1}^{j-1}s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\kappa(\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle \displaystyle=\sum_{u=i+1}^{j-1}s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\kappa(\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\times \displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\times\mathds{1}\Big[\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\leq\tfrac{100C_{A}\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big]\mathds{1}\Big[\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\leq\tfrac{200C_{A}\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big] \displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt+\sum_{u=i+1}^{j-1}s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)(V^{(u-1)}_{j})\kappa\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$($}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$)$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle \displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\times\mathds{1}\Big[\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}>\tfrac{100C_{A}\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\text{ or }\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}>\tfrac{200C_{A}\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big] | $$

Observe that

$$ \displaystyle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}=\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},\widetilde{V}_{i}\rangle-\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\langle V^{(u-1)}_{j},\widetilde{V}_{i}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}} \displaystyle\leq\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},\widetilde{V}_{i}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}+\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\langle V^{(u-1)}_{j},\widetilde{V}_{i}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\leq\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},\widetilde{V}_{i}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}+\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}. $$

Hence, by Corollary 4.3,

$$ \,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}\Big[\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}>\tfrac{100C_{A}\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\text{ or }\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}>\tfrac{200C_{A}\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big]\leq 1-\frac{1}{n^{100}}. | $$

Thus, with probability $1-O(1/n^{100}),$ the second sum is 0 for all $i,j.$

#### Step 6: Martingale analysis.

All that is left to bound is the sum

$$ \begin{split}&\sum_{u=i+1}^{j-1}s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\kappa\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$($}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$)$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\times\\
&\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\times\mathds{1}\Big[|\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle|\leq\tfrac{100C_{A}\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big]\mathds{1}\Big[\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\langle\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$|$}}}\leq\tfrac{100C_{A}\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big].\end{split} $$

Let $K_{u}$ be the term corresponding to $u$ above. We claim that $\{K_{u}\}_{u=i+1}^{j-1}$ is a martingale difference sequence with respect to the filtration in Eq. 5. Measurability follows in the same as way as for $\{M_{u}\}_{u=i+1}^{j-1}$ defined in Lemma 4.4. We also need to show the martingale property.

#### Step 6.1. Martingale property.

For brevity of notation, denote

$$ \displaystyle\mathds{1}(u,j)\coloneqq\mathds{1}\Big[|\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle|\leq\tfrac{100C_{A}\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big] \displaystyle\mathds{1}(u,i,\perp j)\coloneqq\mathds{1}\Big[|\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle|\leq\tfrac{100C_{A}\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big]. $$

We need to show that

$$ \E\Big[s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\kappa(\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\mathds{1}(u,j)\mathds{1}(u,i,\perp j)\Big|\mathcal{F}_{u-1}\Big]=0. $$

This follows immediately from the fact that $\widetilde{V}_{u}$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_{u-1},H_{ju}.$ Hence,

$$ \displaystyle\E\Big[s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\kappa(\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\mathds{1}(u,j)\mathds{1}(u,i,\perp j)\Big|\mathcal{F}_{u-1}\Big] \displaystyle=\E\Big[\E\Big[s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\kappa(\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\times \displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\times\mathds{1}(u,j)\mathds{1}(u,i,\perp j)\Big|\mathcal{F}_{u-1},H_{ju},\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\Big]\;\Big|\mathcal{F}_{u-1}\;\Big] \displaystyle=\E\Big[s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\kappa(\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\mathds{1}(u,j)\times \displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\times\E\Big[\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\mathds{1}(u,i,\perp j)\Big|\mathcal{F}_{u-1},H_{ju},\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\Big]\;\Big|\mathcal{F}_{u-1}\;\Big] $$

We used the fact that $s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle),\mathds{1}(u,j)$ are functions of only $H_{ju},\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle.$ Now, the inner expectation is equal to 0 as the map

$$ V+\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle V^{(u-1)}_{j}\longrightarrow-V+\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle V^{(u-1)}_{j}\,, $$

where $V$ is the component of $\widetilde{V}_{u}$ orthogonal to $V^{(u-1)}_{j}$ , is measure-preserving under the sigma algebra $\sigma\{\mathcal{F}_{u-1},H_{ju},\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\}$ and acts by

$$ \displaystyle\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\mathds{1}\Big[|\langle\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle|\leq\tfrac{100C_{A}\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big] \displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\longrightarrow-\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\mathds{1}\Big[|\langle\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle|\leq\tfrac{100C_{A}\sqrt{\log n}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big]. $$

#### Step 6.2. Martingale concentration.

We end by applying Theorem 2.2. Recall that

$$ K_{u}=s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\kappa\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$($}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$)$}}}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle\mathds{1}(u,j)\mathds{1}(u,i,\perp j) $$

is bounded deterministically by $C^{\prime\prime}\frac{\log n}{d}$ for some absolute constant $C^{\prime\prime}$ due to the indicators and the bound on $\kappa$ from Proposition 4.1. The conditional second moment is at most $(C^{\prime\prime})^{2}p\times\frac{\log^{2}n}{d^{2}}:$

$$ \displaystyle\E[K_{u}^{2}|\mathcal{F}_{u-1}] \displaystyle=\E\Big[\Big(s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\Big)^{2}\kappa(\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)^{2}\langle\widetilde{V}_{u},(\widetilde{V}_{i})^{\perp V^{(u-1)}_{j}}\rangle^{2}\mathds{1}(u,j)\mathds{1}(u,i,\perp j)\Big|\mathcal{F}_{u-1}\Big] \displaystyle\leq\E\Big[\Big(s^{H_{ju}}(\langle{\widetilde{V}_{u}},V^{(u-1)}_{j}\rangle)\Big)^{2}(C^{\prime\prime})^{2}\frac{\log^{2}n}{d^{2}}\Big|\mathcal{F}_{u-1}\Big]\leq(C^{\prime\prime})^{2}p\times\frac{\log^{2}n}{d^{2}}. $$

Altogether, by Theorem 2.2,

$$ \displaystyle\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}\Big[\sum_{u=i+1}^{j-1}K_{u}\geq z\Big] \displaystyle\leq\exp\Big(-\frac{z^{2}/2}{(C^{\prime\prime})^{2}(j-i-1)pd^{-2}\log^{2}n+zC^{\prime\prime}d^{-1}\log n/3}\Big) \displaystyle=\exp\Big(-\frac{z^{2}}{O(np\log^{2}n/d^{2})+O(z\log n/d))}\Big). $$

Taking $z=\frac{c\max(\sqrt{np},\sqrt{\log n})(\log n)^{3/2}}{d}$ for a large enough $c$ makes this last expression $O(1/n^{100}).$

### 4.4 Deriving Corollary 1.1 from Theorem 1.1

#### Proof of Corollary 1.1.

Suppose that one is given the coupling in Theorem 1.1 of $H\sim\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ with vectors $\widetilde{V}_{1},\widetilde{V}_{2},\ldots,\widetilde{V}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$ such that the second condition holds. Thus, with high probability, all edges of the random geometric graph $G_{+}$ defined by

$$ (G_{+})_{ij}=\mathds{1}\Big[\langle\widetilde{V}_{i},\widetilde{V}_{j}\rangle\geq\tau^{p}_{d}-c\max(\sqrt{np},\sqrt{\log n})\frac{(\log n)^{3/2}}{d}\Big] $$

are also edges in $H$ defined by $H_{ji}.$ Note that $G_{+}$ is a sample from $\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p_{+})$ where

$$ p_{+}\coloneqq\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}_{U,V\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}[\langle U,V\rangle\geq\tau^{p}_{d}-c\max(\sqrt{np},\sqrt{\log n})\frac{(\log n)^{3/2}}{d}]. $$

From Lemma 2.1, $p_{+}=p\Big(1+O\Big(\max(\sqrt{np},\sqrt{\log n})\frac{(\log n)^{2}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)\Big).$ Similarly, we consider

$$ (G_{-})_{ij}=\mathds{1}\Big[\langle\widetilde{V}_{i},\widetilde{V}_{j}\rangle\geq\tau^{p}_{d}+\max(\sqrt{np},\sqrt{\log n})\frac{(\log n)^{3/2}}{d}\Big]. $$

Hence, we have a coupling of $H\sim\mathsf{G}(n,p),G_{+}\sim\mathsf{RGG}\Big(n,d,p\Big(1+O\Big(\max(\sqrt{np},\sqrt{\log n})\frac{(\log n)^{2}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)\Big)\Big)$ and $G_{-}\sim\mathsf{RGG}\Big(n,d,p\Big(1-O\Big(\max(\sqrt{np},\sqrt{\log n})\frac{(\log n)^{2}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)\Big)\Big)$ such that $G_{-}\subseteq H\subseteq G_{+}$ with high probability. This is clearly enough. ∎

## 5 Robust Testing

### 5.1 The SoS Program and Refutation

We now give the details for the SoS program. Consider the following axiom set over $n$ $d$ -dimensional variables $(Y_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ stacked together in a $n\times d$ matrix $Y$ and indicator variables $w=(w_{ij})_{1\leq i<j\leq n}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}(Y,w)\coloneqq\begin{cases}\langle Y_{i},Y_{i}\rangle=1\;\forall i,\\
w_{i,j}^{2}=w_{i,j}\;\forall i\neq j,\\
(1-w_{i,j})\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle^{2}\leq(\tau_{d}^{p})^{2}\;\forall i\neq j,\\
\sum_{i,j}w_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle^{2}\leq\frac{2C_{2}n^{2}p\log(1/p)}{d},\end{cases} $$

where $C_{2}$ is the constant from Lemma 2.1. One should interpret the condition imposed by variables $\omega_{ij}$ as a tail bound on the empirical distribution of $\{\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle^{2}\}_{1\leq i<j\leq n}.$ The constraint essentially reads $\sum_{i,j\;:\;\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle^{2}\geq(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2}}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle^{2}\leq\frac{2C_{2}n^{2}p\log(1/p)}{\sqrt{d}},$ which holds w.h.p. when one takes $Y_{i}=V_{i}.$

#### Spectral Refutation Algorithm.

On input a $p$ -centered adjacency matrix $A=A_{G},$ try to prove in degree $12$ SoS that $\Big(\sum_{i,j}A_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2}\leq\frac{n^{4}p^{2}\log(1/p)}{8C_{B}^{2}d},$ where $C_{B}$ is the constant from Lemma 2.1. If the algorithm fails, report that $G$ is a corrupted $\mathsf{RGG}(n,d,p).$ If it succeeds, report that it is a corruption of a graph with small operator norm of its $p$ -centered adjacency matrix (e.g. $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ for concreteness).

### 5.2 Analysis of Corrupted Erdős-Rényi

Let $A$ be the centered adjacency matrix of a corrupted $\mathsf{G}(n,p).$ Let $A=U+S,$ where $U$ is the uncorrupted adjacency matrix and $S$ is defined by $S=A-U.$ The entries of $S$ are in $\{-1,0,1\}$ and at most $\epsilon p\binom{n}{2}$ of them are non-zero ( $S$ is supported on corrupted entries). Hence,

$$ \begin{split}&\Big(\sum_{i,j}A_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2}=\Big(\sum_{i,j}U_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle+\sum_{i,j}S_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2}\\
&=\Big(\sum_{i,j}U_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle+\sum_{i,j}S_{i,j}w_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle+\sum_{i,j}S_{i,j}(1-w_{i,j})\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2}\\
&\leq 4\Big(\sum_{i,j}U_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2}+4\Big(\sum_{i,j}S_{i,j}w_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2}+4\Big(\sum_{i,j}S_{i,j}(1-w_{i,j})\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2},\end{split} $$

where so far all inequalities are in SoS. We bound each of the three terms separately.

#### Case 1) Uncorrupted value:

Note that $\sum_{i,j}U_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle=\langle U,Y^{T}Y\rangle.$ Since $U$ is the signed adjacency matrix of $\mathsf{G}(n,p),$ with high probability $\lambda_{\max}(U)\leq C\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)$ for some absolute constant $C$ by Theorem 2.1. Hence, $C\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)I-U\succeq 0$ and, thus, in SoS,

$$ \displaystyle\langle U,YY^{T}\rangle\leq\langle C\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)I,YY^{T}\rangle=C\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\times\mathsf{tr}(YY^{T})=C\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\times n. $$

Similarly, $\langle U,YY^{T}\rangle\geq-C\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\times n.$ Thus, in SoS, $\Big(\sum_{i,j}U_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2}\leq C^{2}\max({n^{3}p},n^{2}\log^{2}n).$

#### Case 2)

Corrupted value with large entries. By Cauchy-Schwartz inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\Big(\sum_{i,j}S_{i,j}w_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2} \displaystyle\leq\Big(\sum_{i,j}S_{i,j}^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{i,j}w_{i,j}^{2}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle^{2}\Big) \displaystyle\leq\Big(\sum_{i,j\;:\;(ij)\text{ corrupted}}1\Big)\Big(\sum_{i,j}w_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle^{2}\Big) \displaystyle\leq\epsilon pn^{2}\times\frac{4C_{2}^{2}n^{2}p\log(1/p)}{d}. $$

#### Case 3)

Corrupted value with small entries. Again, by Cauchy-Schwartz,

$$ \displaystyle\Big(\sum_{i,j}S_{i,j}(1-w_{i,j})\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2} \displaystyle=\Big(\sum_{i,j}S^{3}_{i,j}(1-w_{i,j})\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2} \displaystyle\leq\Big(\sum_{i,j}S_{i,j}^{2}\Big)\Big(S_{i,j}^{4}\sum_{i,j}(1-w_{i,j})^{2}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle^{2}\Big) \displaystyle\leq\epsilon pn^{2}\times\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}S_{i,j}^{4}(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2} \displaystyle\leq\epsilon pn^{2}\times\epsilon pn^{2}\times(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2}\leq\frac{C_{A}^{2}\epsilon^{2}n^{4}p^{2}\log(1/p)}{d}, $$

using Lemma 2.1. Altogether, for some absolute constant $C^{\prime},$ when $A$ is an $\epsilon$ -corruption of $\mathsf{G}(n,p),$ with high probability there is a degree 12 proof in SoS that

$$ \displaystyle\Big(\sum_{i,j}A_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2}\leq C^{\prime}\Big(\max(n^{3}p,n^{2}\log^{2}n)+\frac{\epsilon n^{4}p^{2}\log(1/p)}{d}\Big). $$

### 5.3 Analysis of Corrupted RGG

We will show that with high probability over $\mathsf{RGG}(n,d,p),$ for no $\epsilon$ -corruption $A$ can one prove $\Big(\sum_{i,j}A_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2}\leq\frac{n^{4}p^{2}\log(1/p)}{d}.$ We simply need to exhibit a pair $(Y,w)$ that satisfies the axioms $\mathcal{A}(Y,w)$ and $\Big(\sum_{i,j}A_{i,j}\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2}\geq\frac{n^{4}p^{2}\log(1/p)}{8C_{B}^{2}d}.$

Let $Y_{i}=V_{i},1\leq i\leq n,$ where this is the true embedding that produced $A.$ Let $w_{i,j}=\mathds{1}[\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle^{2}\geq(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2}].$

#### Feasibility.

Clearly, the first three axioms are satisfied. For the last one,

$$ \displaystyle\E_{V_{1},V_{2},\ldots,V_{n}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\sum_{i\neq j}\mathds{1}[\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle^{2}\geq(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2}]\times\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle^{2}\Big] \displaystyle\leq n^{2}\E_{V_{1},V_{2}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\mathds{1}[\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle^{2}\geq(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2}]\times\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle^{2}\Big] \displaystyle=n^{2}\E_{V_{1},V_{2}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle^{2}|\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle^{2}\geq(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2}\Big]\times\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}\Big[\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle^{2}\geq(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2}\Big] \displaystyle\leq n^{2}p\times\frac{C_{2}^{2}\log(1/p)}{d} $$

by Lemma 2.1. Furthermore, the value concentrates extremely well as the collection of random variables $\{\mathds{1}[\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle^{2}\geq(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2}]\times\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle^{2}\}_{1\leq i<j\leq n}$ is pairwise independent! (Note that $\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle$ and $\langle V_{2},V_{3}\rangle$ are independent.) Hence,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{V}_{V_{1},V_{2},\ldots,V_{n}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\sum_{i\neq j}\mathds{1}[\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle^{2}\geq(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2}]\times\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle^{2}\Big] \displaystyle\leq n^{2}\mathbb{V}_{V_{1},V_{2}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\mathds{1}[\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle^{2}\geq(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2}]\times\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle^{2}\Big] \displaystyle\leq n^{2}\E_{V_{1},V_{2}\sim_{iid}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}\Big[\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle^{4}|\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle^{2}\geq(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2}\Big]\times\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}\Big[\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle^{2}\geq(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2}\Big] \displaystyle\leq n^{2}p\times\frac{C_{4}\log(1/p)^{2}}{d^{2}}=o\bigg(\Big(n^{2}p\times\frac{C_{2}^{2}\log(1/p)}{d}\Big)^{2}\bigg). $$

Hence, $\sum_{i\neq j}\mathds{1}[\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle^{2}\geq(\tau^{p}_{d})^{2}]\times\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle^{2}\leq\frac{2C^{2}_{2}n^{2}p\log(1/p)}{d}$ w.h.p. by Chebyshev’s inequality.

#### Objective Value.

Finally, we need to bound $\sum_{i,j}A_{i,j}\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle.$ As in the Erdős-Rényi case,

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\sum_{i,j}S_{i,j}\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\Big|\leq 2\sqrt{\Big(\sum_{i,j}S_{i,j}w_{i,j}\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2}+\Big(\sum_{i,j}S_{i,j}(1-w_{i,j})\langle Y_{i},Y_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2}} \displaystyle\leq 2\sqrt{\epsilon pn^{2}\times\frac{4C_{2}^{2}n^{2}p\log(1/p)}{d}+\frac{C_{A}^{2}\epsilon^{2}n^{4}p^{2}\log(1/p)}{d}}\leq\frac{C^{\prime\prime}\sqrt{\epsilon}n^{2}p\sqrt{\log(1/p)}}{\sqrt{d}}. $$

Hence, we only need to show that $\sum_{i,j}U_{i,j}\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle$ is large. Again, as the different summands are pairwise independent and this value concentrates well, we only consider the expectation:

$$ \displaystyle\E\Big[\sum_{i,j}U_{i,j}\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\Big] \displaystyle=n(n-1)\E\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$[$}}}\mathds{1}[\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\geq\tau^{p}_{d}]\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$]$}}} \displaystyle=n(n-1)\E\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$[$}}}\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle|\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\geq\tau^{p}_{d}\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$]$}}}\times\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$[$}}}\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\geq\tau^{p}_{d}\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$]$}}} \displaystyle\geq n(n-1)p\E\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$[$}}}\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle|\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\geq\tau^{p}_{d}\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$]$}}}\geq\frac{n^{2}p\sqrt{\log(1/p)}}{2C_{B}\sqrt{d}}, $$

the last inequality by Lemma 2.1. Hence, $\sum_{i,j}A_{i,j}\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\geq\frac{n^{2}p\sqrt{\log(1/p)}}{2C_{B}\sqrt{d}}-\frac{C^{\prime\prime}\sqrt{\epsilon}n^{2}p\sqrt{\log(1/p)}}{\sqrt{d}}$ and so $\Big(\sum_{i,j}A_{i,j}\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\Big)^{2}\geq\frac{n^{4}p^{2}\log(1/p)}{8C^{2}_{B}d}$ for all $\epsilon\leq K_{r}^{\prime}$ for some absolute constant $K_{r}^{\prime}.$

### 5.4 Putting It All Together

By the previous two sections, as long as $\frac{n^{4}p^{2}\log(1/p)}{8C^{2}_{B}d}\geq C^{\prime}\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$($}}}\max(n^{3}p,n^{2}\log^{2}n)+\frac{\epsilon n^{4}p^{2}\log(1/p)}{d}\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$)$}}},$ the test succeeds with high probability. This occurs if $\epsilon\leq K_{r}$ and $d\leq K_{r}\min(np\log(1/p),n^{2}p^{2}\log(1/p)\log^{-2}n)$ for some absolute constant $C.$

#### Remark 6.

The only property needed about the $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ distribution in Theorem 1.3 is that for the centered adjacency matrix $U$ of a sample from $\mathsf{G}(n,p),$ $|\lambda_{\max}(U)|\leq c_{1}\frac{n^{3}p^{2}\log(1/p)}{d}.$ Hence, our result holds for robust testing between ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}$ and any distribution $\mathcal{G}$ for which the $p$ -centered adjacency matrix of a sample from $\mathcal{G}$ has operator norm at most $c_{1}\frac{n^{3}p^{2}\log(1/p)}{d}$ for some absolute constant $c_{1}.$

## 6 Enumerating Geometric Graphs and the Support Size of RGG

#### Proof of Theorem 1.4.

Suppose that we are given some $d\geq\log^{7}n$ (otherwise, the theorem statement follows immediately from the 2-dimensional case by [MM11]).

Take $p=d/(n\log^{6.5}n)=\Omega(1/n).$ Now, Theorem 1.1 implies that there exists a coupling of $H\sim\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ and $V_{1},V_{2},\ldots,V_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$ such that with high probability:

- 1. $\mathds{1}\Big[\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\geq\tau^{p}_{d}-c\frac{\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\log n^{3/2}}{d}\Big]\geq H_{i,j}$ for all $i,j.$

- 2. $\mathds{1}\Big[\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\geq\tau^{p}_{d}+c\frac{\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\log n^{3/2}}{d}\Big]\leq H_{i,j}$ for all $i,j.$

Thus, the random geometric graph $G$ defined by $G_{i,j}=\mathds{1}\Big[\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\geq\tau^{p}_{d}-c\frac{\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\log n^{3/2}}{d}\Big]$ has $H$ as an edge-subgraph. $G$ is a sample from $\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p(1+\delta)),$ where

$$ p\delta=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}_{X\sim\mathcal{D}_{d}}\Big[X\in\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$[$}}}\tau^{p}_{d}-c\tfrac{\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\log n^{3/2}}{d},\tau^{p}_{d}\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$]$}}}\Big]. $$

By Part D) of Lemma 2.1, $\delta=O\Big(\frac{\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\log n^{3/2}{\log(1/p)^{1/2}}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)=o(1).$

Furthermore, as $\mathds{1}\Big[\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\geq\tau^{p}_{d}+c\frac{\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\log n^{3/2}}{d}\Big]\leq H_{i,j}$ for all $i,j,$ it is the case that $G\setminus H$ is a set of edges which belongs to the edge-set defined by

$$ \displaystyle\Big\{(i,j)\;:\;\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\in\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$[$}}}\tau^{p}_{d}-c\tfrac{\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\log n^{3/2}}{d},\tau^{p}_{d}+c\tfrac{\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\log n^{3/2}}{d}\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$]$}}}\Big\}. $$

By Part D) of Lemma 2.1, $q\coloneqq\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}\Big[\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\in\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$[$}}}\tau^{p}_{d}-c\frac{\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\log n^{3/2}}{d},\tau^{p}_{d}+c\frac{\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\log n^{3/2}}{d}\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$]$}}}\Big]=O\Big(p\frac{\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\log n^{3/2}{\log(1/p)^{1/2}}}{\sqrt{d}}\Big)=o(p).$ Hence, in expectation, $G\setminus H$ is contained in a set of size $o(n^{2}p).$ Note that the events $\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\{$}}}\langle V_{i},V_{j}\rangle\in\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$[$}}}\tau^{p}_{d}-c\frac{\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\log n^{3/2}}{d},\tau^{p}_{d}+c\frac{\max(\sqrt{np},\log n)\log n^{3/2}}{d}\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$]$}}}\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\}$}}}_{i\neq j}$ are pairwise independent. Hence, by the second moment method, with high probability the set in Eq. 10 is of cardinality at most $2\max(q,1/n^{3/2})n^{2}=o(pn^{2}).$ We reach the following conclusion.

#### Corollary 6.1.

For $G\sim\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p(1+\delta)),H\sim\mathsf{G}(n,p),$ coupled as above, with high probability, $H\text{ is an edge-subgraph of $G$}\text{ and }|E(G)|-|E(H)|\leq\epsilon n^{2}p\text{ for some }\epsilon=o(1).$

This is enough to conclude that $\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p(1+\delta))$ has support of size $\exp(\Omega(n^{2}p\log(1/p)))=\exp(\Omega(nd\log n^{-7}))$ using the following two nearly trivial observations proved in Appendix B.

#### Observation 6.2 ([BB23, Implicit in Theorem 7.5.]).

Suppose that $p\leq 1/2,p=\Omega(1/n).$ Then, any set $A$ such that $P_{H\sim\mathsf{G}(n,p)}[H\in A]\geq 1/2$ satisfies $|A|\geq\exp(\frac{1}{6}n^{2}p\log(1/p)).$

#### Observation 6.3.

Suppose that $p\leq 1/2,p=\Omega(1/n)$ and $\epsilon<1/100.$ Let $G$ be any graph on at most $n^{2}p$ edges. Then, the number of edge-subgraphs $H$ of $G$ such that $|E(G)|-|E(H)|\leq\epsilon n^{2}p$ is at most $\exp(2n^{2}p\epsilon\log(1/\epsilon)).$

With probability more than $1/2,$ it is the case that $H$ is an edge-subgraph of $G$ by Corollary 6.1 and $G$ has at most $2\binom{n}{2}p\leq n^{2}p$ edges (again, edges of random geometric graphs are pairwise-independent). Let $B$ be the support of $\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p(1+\delta)$ restricted to graphs on at most $n^{2}p$ edges. Hence, the number of edge-subgraphs of graphs in $B$ which differ in at most $\epsilon n^{2}p$ edges is at most $|B|\times\exp(2n^{2}p\epsilon\log(1/\epsilon))=|B|\times\exp(o(n^{2}p\log(1/p)))$ by Observation 6.3. By Observation 6.2, $|B|\times\exp(o(n^{2}p\log(1/p)))\geq\exp(\frac{1}{6}n^{2}p\log(1/p)).$ Hence, $|B|\geq\exp(\frac{1}{7}n^{2}p\log(1/p))=\exp(\Omega(n^{2}d\log^{-7}n)).$ ∎

#### Remark 7 (On The Support Size of The RGG distribution).

The argument above shows that whenever $d\geq\max(np,\log^{2}n)\log(n)^{3}\log(1/p),$ the $\mathsf{RGG}$ distribution is supported on $\exp(\Omega(n^{2}p\log(1/p)))$ graphs. Whenever $d\leq np\log(1/p)\log(n)^{-1},$ it is supported on $\exp(o(n^{2}p\log(1/p)))$ as the number of geometric graphs in dimension $d$ is $\exp(o(nd\log n))$ [MM11, Sau21]. In particular, just like our spectral refutation algorithm shows (see Remark 3), this means that a coupling of the form $H_{-}\subseteq G\subseteq H_{+}$ cannot exist when $d\leq np\log(1/p)\log(n)^{-1}.$

## 7 Sharp Thresholds

### 7.1 Proof of Theorem 1.2

#### Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Consider some monotone property $\mathcal{P}_{n}$ such that $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ exhibits sharp thresholds for $\mathcal{P}_{n}.$ For any constant $\epsilon>0,$ let the critical window $\omega_{\epsilon}$ be of length $o_{n}(p).$ Let $f:[0,1]\longrightarrow[0,1]$ be the function defined by $f(p)=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}_{\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{G}(n,p)}[\mathbf{G}\in\mathcal{P}].$ Let $p_{n}^{c}=f^{-1}(1/2).$ Similarly, let $g(p)=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}_{\mathbf{G}\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}}[\mathbf{G}\in\mathcal{P}].$ Let $q_{n}^{c}=g^{-1}(1/2).$

Take $\delta\in(0,0.1)$ to be any absolute constant. Since $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ exhibits sharp thresholds with respect to $\mathcal{P},$ $f^{-1}(\epsilon(1-\delta))=p(1+o_{n}(1)).$ Now, by Corollary 1.1, one can couple with high probability $1-\psi$ for some $\psi=o(1)=o(\epsilon\delta),$ the graphs $\mathbf{G}_{-}\sim\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},f^{-1}(\epsilon(1-\delta))\times(1-\frac{c\max(\sqrt{np^{c}_{n}},\sqrt{\log n})(\log^{2}n)}{\sqrt{d}})$ and $\mathbf{H}_{-}\sim\mathsf{G}(n,f^{-1}(\epsilon(1-\delta))).$ Hence, as $\mathcal{P}_{n}$ is monotone,

$$ \,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{-}\in\mathcal{P}_{n}]\leq\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{-}\not\subseteq\mathbf{H}_{-}]+\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{-}\subseteq\mathbf{H}_{-},\mathbf{H}_{-}\in\mathcal{P}_{n}]\leq\psi+\epsilon(1-\delta)\leq\epsilon. $$

Hence, $g^{-1}(\epsilon)\geq f^{-1}(\epsilon(1-\delta))\times(1-\frac{c\max(\sqrt{np^{c}_{n}},\sqrt{\log n})(\log^{2}n)}{\sqrt{d}})=f^{-1}(\epsilon(1-\delta))(1-o_{n}(1)).$ As this holds for any $\delta>0,$ $g^{-1}(\epsilon)\geq f^{-1}(\epsilon(1-o_{n}(1)))(1-o_{n}(1)).$ Similarly, $g^{-1}(1-\epsilon)\leq f^{-1}(1-\epsilon(1-o_{n}(1)))(1+o_{n}(1)).$

Altogether, this means that

$$ g(1-\epsilon)-g(\epsilon)=o(f^{-1}(1-\epsilon(1-o_{n}(1))))+o(f^{-1}(\epsilon(1-o_{n}(1))))+f^{-1}(1-\epsilon(1-o_{n}(1)))-f^{-1}(\epsilon(1-o_{n}(1)))=o(p_{n}^{c}). $$

Taking $\epsilon\longrightarrow 1/2$ in

$$ f^{-1}((1-\epsilon)(1-o_{n}(1)))(1-o_{n}(1))\leq g^{-1}(1-\epsilon)\leq f^{-1}(1-\epsilon(1-o_{n}(1)))(1+o_{n}(1)) $$

also implies that $q_{n}^{c}=p_{n}^{c}(1+o(1)).$ ∎

### 7.2 RGG and the FKG Lattice Condition

A measure $\mu$ over $\{0,1\}^{N}$ is strictly positive if $\mu(\omega)>0$ for each $\omega\in\{0,1\}^{n}.$ A strictly positive measure satisfies the FKG lattice condition if for any two $\omega_{1},\omega_{2}\in\{0,1\}^{N},$ it holds that $\mu(\omega_{1}\vee\omega_{2})\mu(\omega_{1}\wedge\omega_{2})\geq\mu(\omega_{1})\mu(\omega_{2})$ [GG06]. We denote pointwise maximum with $\vee$ and pointwise minimum with $\wedge.$

#### Proposition 7.1.

Suppose that $d\geq 3.$ Then, the measure corresponding to $\mathsf{RGG}(3,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},1/2)$ is strictly positive but does not satisfy the FKG lattice property.

#### Proof.

Denote by $\mu$ the measure corresponding to $\mathsf{RGG}(3,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},1/2).$ Due to symmetry, note that $\mu(\omega)$ only depends on $|\omega|.$ For simplicity of notation, we will also write $\mu(|\omega|)$ for $\mu(\omega).$

We will prove that for some $a\in(0,1/8),$ it is the case that

$$ \displaystyle\mu(3)=1/8+a,\mu(2)=1/8-a,\mu(1)=1/8+a,\mu(0)=1/8-a. $$

This is enough to show that the FKG lattice condition does not hold. Indeed, take $\omega_{1}=\{(1,2)\},\omega_{2}=\{(2,3)\}.$ Then, $\omega_{1}\vee\omega_{2}=\{(1,2),(2,3)\},\omega_{1}\wedge\omega_{2}=\emptyset.$ For the FKG lattice property to hold, it must be the case that $\mu(2)\mu(0)\geq\mu(1)^{2}.$ This, however, is false as the left hand-side is $(1/8-a)^{2}$ while the right hand-side is $(1/8+a)^{2}.$

Going back to Eq. 11. Let $\mu(3)=1/8+a,$ where $a$ is for now some number that we will later prove to be strictly positive. First, note that

$$ \mu(3)+\mu(2)=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{12}=1,\mathbf{G}_{13}=1,\mathbf{G}_{23}=1]+\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{12}=1,\mathbf{G}_{13}=1,\mathbf{G}_{23}=0]=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{12}=1,\mathbf{G}_{13}=1]. $$

The last expression equals $1/4$ as every two edges in ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}$ are pairwise independent. Hence, $\mu(2)=1/4-\mu(3)=1/8-a.$ Similarly, $\mu(1)=1/4-\mu(2)=1/8+a$ as

$$ \mu(2)+\mu(1)=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{12}=1,\mathbf{G}_{13}=1,\mathbf{G}_{23}=0]+\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{12}=1,\mathbf{G}_{13}=0,\mathbf{G}_{23}=0]=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{12}=1,\mathbf{G}_{23}=0], $$

and $\mu(0)=1/4-\mu(1)=1/8-a$ as

$$ \mu(1)+\mu(0)=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{12}=1,\mathbf{G}_{13}=0,\mathbf{G}_{23}=0]+\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{12}=0,\mathbf{G}_{13}=0,\mathbf{G}_{23}=0]=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{13}=0,\mathbf{G}_{23}=0]. $$

Thus, all that is left to show is that $a\geq 0.$ We accomplish this by bounding $\mu(3).$

$$ \displaystyle\mu(3)=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{12}=1,\mathbf{G}_{13}=1,\mathbf{G}_{23}=1] \displaystyle=\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{23}=1|\mathbf{G}_{12}=1,\mathbf{G}_{13}=1]\times\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{12}=1,\mathbf{G}_{13}=1] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\mathbf{G}_{23}=1|\mathbf{G}_{12}=1,\mathbf{G}_{13}=1] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[\langle V_{2},V_{3}\rangle\geq 0|\langle V_{1},V_{2}\rangle\geq 0,\langle V_{1},V_{3}\rangle\geq 0]. $$

First, note that this probability is the same if $V_{1},V_{2},V_{3}$ were isotropic Gaussian vectors instead of spherical - the sign of inner products depends only on the direction but not on the magnitude of vectors. Due to rotational invariance, we can assume that $V_{1}\in\mathsf{span}\{e_{1}\},$ so $V_{1}=z_{1,1}e_{1},$ where $z_{1,1}>0,$ and $V_{2}\in\mathsf{span}\{e_{1},e_{2}\}.$ So, $V_{2}=z_{2,1}e_{1}+z_{2,2}e_{2}.$ Finally, let $V_{3}=z_{3,1}e_{1}+z_{3,2}e_{2}+z_{3,3}e_{3}.$ Since the components of an isotropic Gaussian are are independent in different directions, all of the numbers $z_{1,1},z_{2,1},z_{2,2},z_{3,1},z_{3,2},z_{3,3}$ are independent, Furthermore, $z_{2,1},z_{3,1},z_{3,2}$ are standard Gaussians and $z_{1,1},z_{2,2},z_{3,3}>0$ as these are norms of certain projections of the Gaussian vectors. We want to show that

$$ \,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[z_{3,1}z_{2,1}+z_{3,2}z_{2,2}\geq 0|z_{3,1}\geq 0,z_{2,1}\geq 0]\in(1/2,1). $$

We compute

$$ \displaystyle\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[z_{3,1}z_{2,1}+z_{3,2}z_{2,2}\geq 0|z_{3,1}\geq 0,z_{2,1}\geq 0] \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{+\infty}\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[z_{3,1}z_{2,1}+z_{3,2}z_{2,2}\geq 0|z_{3,1}\geq 0,z_{2,1}\geq 0,z_{3,1}z_{2,1}=x]\times\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[z_{3,1}z_{2,1}=x|z_{3,1}\geq 0,z_{2,1}\geq 0]dx \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{+\infty}\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[z_{3,2}\geq-x/z_{2,2}]\times\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[z_{3,1}z_{2,1}=x|z_{3,1}\geq 0,z_{2,1}\geq 0]dx. $$

Note that for each $x,z_{2,2}\geq 0,$ it holds that $\,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[z_{3,2}\geq-x/z_{2,2}]\in(1/2,1)$ as $z_{3,2}$ is a standard Gaussian and $-x/z_{2,2}<0.$ The conclusion follows. ∎

## 8 Discussion and Open Problems

### 8.1 Robust Testing With Fewer Corruptions

One of the main results of the current paper is settling (up to log factors) the regime in which testing between $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ and ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}$ with $\epsilon\binom{n}{2}p$ corruptions is possible when $\epsilon>0$ is a small constant. We show via Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 that the threshold is $d=\widetilde{\Theta}(np)$ both computationally and information-theoretically. The analogous question without corruptions, i.e. $\epsilon=0,$ is still open as discussed in the introduction. It is natural to interpolate between $\epsilon=0$ and $\epsilon=\Theta(1).$

#### Problem 2.

Given are $n,d\in\mathbb{N},$ $p\in[0,1]$ and a function $\epsilon(n,p)\geq 0$ such that $\epsilon(n,p)\leq K_{r}$ for some universal constant $K_{r}.$ Consider the following hypothesis testing problem. One observes a graph $H$ and needs to decide between $H_{0}:H=\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{G}),\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ and $H_{1}:H=\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{G}),\mathbf{G}\sim\mathsf{RGG}(n,d,p).$ Here, $\mathcal{A}:\{0,1\}^{\binom{n}{2}}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{\binom{n}{2}}$ is any unknown mapping such that $\mathcal{A}(G)$ and $G$ differ in at most $\epsilon(n,p)\times\binom{n}{2}p$ entries for any adjacency matrix $G\in\{0,1\}^{\binom{n}{2}}.$

We expect that this question will require both novel algorithmic and lower-bound ideas. Neither the spectral refutation algorithm (when $\epsilon=\Theta(1)$ ) nor the signed triangle count algorithm (when $\epsilon=0$ ) seems to generalize trivially. Regarding lower-bounds, even the case of no corruptions is still open. Particularly interesting is whether there is a statistical-computational gap for any $\epsilon(n,p).$ There is no evidence for such a gap when $\epsilon(n,p)=0$ and $\epsilon(n,p)=\Theta(1).$

Theorems 1.1 and 1.1 show that if $\epsilon(n,p)\geq C\frac{\max(\sqrt{np},\sqrt{\log n})(\log n)^{2}}{\sqrt{d}}$ for some absolute constant $C,$ the distinguishing problem is impossible information theoretically against the (efficient) adversary from Theorem 1.1. We do not expect this to be tight for all values of $\epsilon$ (in particular, when $\epsilon$ approaches 0). This naturally also raises a question about the optimality of Theorems 1.1 and 1.1. We only phrase the question for the latter.

#### Problem 3.

What is the smallest value of $\delta(d,n,p)$ for which there exists a coupling of $G\sim\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p),$ $H_{-}\sim\mathsf{G}(n,p(1-\delta(d,n,p)))$ and $H_{+}\sim\mathsf{G}(n,p(1+\delta(d,n,p))),$ such that $H_{-}\subseteq G\subseteq H_{+}$ with high-probability.

### 8.2 Embedding Random Geometric Graphs

#### New Algorithms For Embedding.

Theorem 1.1 can also be viewed as an approximate embedding of a sample $H$ from $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ as a geometric graph. This naturally raises the question whether one can use Algorithm 1 to embed a sample $H$ from ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}$ (with the true vectors remaining unknown). Our martingale-based analysis fails in this scenario as the independence of variables $H_{ji}$ is crucial. Nevertheless, the fact that the marginal distribution of vectors $V_{1},V_{2},\ldots,V_{n}$ is uniform and independent makes such an algorithm extremely appealing as it gives a certain sampling flavor of the resulting embedding: It produces a uniform sample from a certain set of $n$ -tuples of latent vectors which nearly match the input adjacency matrix.

#### Robust Embedding.

A different algorithmic question is whether there exist embedding algorithms in the setting of adversarial corruptions. One way to phrase this question (using a Frobenius norm error) is:

#### Problem 4.

Let $V=(V_{1},V_{2},\ldots,V_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ where $V_{1},V_{2},\ldots,V_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathsf{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$ and $G$ be the corresponding geometric graph with $\epsilon\binom{n}{2}p$ edge corruptions (or $\epsilon n$ node corruptions). On input $G,$ find a matrix $\widehat{W}$ such that $\|\widehat{W}-V^{T}V\|_{F}=\|V^{T}V\|_{F}\times(f(\epsilon)+o(1)),$ where $f(\epsilon)$ is some function such that $\lim_{\epsilon\longrightarrow 0}f(\epsilon)=0.$

The case of no corruptions (i.e. $\epsilon=0$ ) is treated in [LS23] via a spectral algorithm which succeeds whenever $d=o(np).$

### 8.3 A Reverse Coupling?

Algorithm 1 efficiently couples with high probability a sample $H$ from $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ and a sample $G$ from ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}$ on input $H$ such that they differ on $o(n^{2}p)$ edges. One may naturally ask the question of whether such an efficient coupling algorithm exists on input the random geometric graph.

#### Problem 5.

Design an efficient algorithm which on input $G\sim{\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}$ where $d\geq np\times\log^{C}n$ for an appropriate constant $C$ produces a graph $H(G)$ such that:

- 1. ${d_{\mathsf{TV}}}(\mathcal{L}(H(G)),\mathsf{G}(n,p))=o(1).$

- 2. With high probability, $H(G)$ and $G$ differ on $o(n^{2}p)$ edges.

The question is only about efficiency as one can simply reverse the coupling in Theorem 1.1.

### 8.4 Other Random Geometric Graph Distributions

We showed that the central result of the current paper Theorem 1.1 has a wide range of applications, including to robust statistics, enumeration, and sharp thresholds. The proof technique, however, is specialized to spherical random geometric graphs. Naturally, one may want a more systematic approach which also works for other high-dimensional random geometric graphs such as over the torus [BB24a] or Boolean hypercube [BB23] or non-uniform distributions such as the anisotropic random geometric graphs in [EM20, BBH24]. We believe that extending our results and techniques to other geometries is an exciting open direction. Our only progress in that direction is for Gaussian random geometric graphs, which is nearly identical to the spherical case.

#### Remark 8.

Corollaries 1.1 and 1.1 hold with the exact same parameters (up to multiplicative constants) for Gaussian RGG. A sample from ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}$ is an $n$ -vertex graph $G$ defined by sampling $Z_{1},Z_{2},\ldots,Z_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d})$ and setting $G_{ji}=\mathds{1}[\langle Z_{i},Z_{j}\rangle\geq\xi^{p}_{d}]$ where $\xi^{p}_{d}$ is such that the expected density is $p.$ One coupling algorithm is Algorithm 1 except that at the end one defines $Z^{(i-1)}_{i}=\chi_{i}\times V^{(i-1)}_{i},$ where the variables $(\chi_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ are independent of everything else and are distributed as $\|\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d})\|_{2}.$ Now, use that $|\chi_{i}-1|\leq\frac{\log n}{\sqrt{d}}$ with high probability (e.g. [BB24b]) and the fact that $|\tau^{p}_{d}-\xi^{p}_{d}|=\widetilde{O}(1/d)$ [BB24b]. One immediately concludes that when $d\gg np,$ the robust testing Problem 1 is information theoretically impossible. This is perhaps surprising in the sparse case due to the difference between spherical and Gaussian RGG [BB24b]. There is an efficient test that distinguishes ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}$ and $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ when $d\gg n^{3/2}p,p=O(n^{-3/4})$ [BB24b] in the case of no corruptions, a regime in which ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}$ and $\mathsf{G}(n,p)$ are conjectured to be information-theoretically indistinguishable. Yet, when testing with adversarial corruptions no such difference between ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}),p)}$ and ${\mathsf{RGG}(n,\mathbb{S}^{d-1},p)}$ seems to emerge.

On the other hand, for any fixed graph $K$ on at least $\frac{1}{2}\E|E(H)|=\frac{1}{2}\binom{n}{2}p$ vertices, we have

$$ \,{\rm I}\kern-1.66492pt{\rm P}[H=K]=p^{|E(K)|}(1-p)^{\binom{n}{2}-|E(K)|}\leq p^{|E(K)|}\leq\exp\Big(\log p\frac{1}{2}\binom{n}{2}p\Big)\leq\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{5}n^{2}p\log\frac{1}{p}\Big). $$

Hence, a $1/2-o(1)$ mass of the set $A$ must be supported on graphs with mass $\exp\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$($}}}-\frac{1}{5}n^{2}p\log\frac{1}{p}\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$)$}}}$ each with respect to $\mathsf{G}(n,p).$ The statement follows. ∎

#### Proof of Observation 6.3.

The number of such subgraphs of $H$ is simply $\sum_{r=0}^{\epsilon n^{2}p}\binom{|E(H)|}{r}.$ We can trivially bound

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{\epsilon n^{2}p}\binom{|E(H)|}{r} \displaystyle\leq\sum_{r=0}^{\epsilon n^{2}p}\binom{n^{2}p}{r}\leq\epsilon n^{2}p\binom{n^{2}p}{\epsilon n^{2}p} \displaystyle\leq\epsilon n^{2}p\Big(\frac{en^{2}p}{\epsilon n^{2}p}\Big)^{\epsilon n^{2}p}=\epsilon n^{2}p(e/\epsilon)^{\epsilon n^{2}p}\leq\exp(2n^{2}p\epsilon\log(1/\epsilon)).\qed $$
